newsitem.title: CANADA: CUSTOM GRAIN ORDERS IN CANADA'S FUTURE - CARGILL LTD.
newsitem.headline: CUSTOM GRAIN ORDERS IN CANADA'S FUTURE - CARGILL LTD.

text.p: Canada's bulk grain handling and transport system will need to change to meet a growing trend toward processors' custom orders if it is to thrive, a Canadian grain industry leader said on Monday.

"Processors are going to pick out pieces of what's growing out there to suit their individual needs, they're doing that today," Cargill Ltd president Kerry Hawkins told Reuters in an interview on Monday. "Unfortunately, the system is homogeneous and generic ... it's very difficult for us to manage those special customer requirements."

Cargill Ltd, a unit of U.S.-based Cargill Inc, is one of Canada's largest grain handlers, meat packers and oilseed processors with sales of C$4.0 billion in fiscal 1996 (June/May) versus C$3.2 billion in 1995.
"With computers and communicating with consumers, grain companies and farmers, we're going to be able to do a much better job of giving customers what they want," Hawkins said.
Three billion to four billion people within 15 years should be able to afford food they cannot currently buy, he said.
"That's a tremendous opportunity and on an absolute basis, there are no new acres coming into production," he added.
Canada exported C$17.3 billion in agricultural goods in 1995 with wheat making up 23 percent of shipments, meat at 19 percent and canola at eight percent, according to Agriculture Canada data.
Overseas millers on tour in Winnipeg earlier this summer said they would prefer to track grain from the source.

"There's no way to match a railcar report with a vessel. We look for predictability in grain quality specifications because we don't always get consistent functionality and there is no mechanism to address this to mitigate our losses in competitiveness," Singapore's Prima Flour Mills Ltd research manager Lim Kay Kong said on June 20.

Hawkins said that farmers will need to resist the urge of swinging en-masse to and from grain and oilseed production as dictated by price spreads between commodities prior to seeding and instead anticipate consumer needs in advance.

To that end, Canada needs to set up a responsive and fail-safe grain transport system while lobbying individual nations and at the next round of World Trade Organization agriculture negotiations for more market liberalization, he said.
